issues.problem: no[1] defines CYOD incorrectly: 'CYOD still means the company chooses from approved models'. In CYOD the EMPLOYEE chooses from a company-approved list (the device is normally still corporate-owned). The `why` also expands COPE as 'company-owned, personally enabled'; CompTIA's acronym list and Messer use 'corporate-owned, personally enabled'.
issues.fix: Replace no[1] with: "CYOD lets the employee pick a device from a company-approved list. Nothing here says the manager chooses the model; the defining facts are company-purchased with personal use allowed, which is COPE." In `why`, change 'company-owned, personally enabled' to 'corporate-owned, personally enabled'.

issues.problem: Blank [2] has more than one true answer. With [1]=containment, the sentence 'responders usually move to containment before [2]' is true for eradication, recovery AND lessons learned (all three options come after containment). Only 'eradication' is keyed, so a learner picking 'recovery' or 'lessons learned' is marked wrong for a true statement. Blank [1] has the same weakness in reverse if [2] is filled with a later phase (eradication also comes before recovery).
issues.fix: Change text to: "After detection and analysis, the next phase is [1]. The phase that comes immediately after that is [2]." Keep blanks as [["containment","eradication","recovery"],["eradication","recovery","lessons learned"]].

issues.problem: Example says 'Alder lists its cloud mail provider in SPF so lookalike senders fail the check.' SPF only checks whether the sending server is authorized for the domain actually used in the envelope sender. A lookalike (cousin) domain is a different domain with its own SPF record and can pass SPF. The sentence teaches that SPF stops lookalike domains, which it does not.
issues.fix: Replace example with: "Alder lists its cloud mail provider in SPF so mail sent from any other server claiming to be from Alder's domain fails the check."

issues.problem: 'reject mail that fails SPF or DKIM checks' is loose: DMARC fails a message only when neither SPF nor DKIM produces an aligned pass. A message that fails SPF but passes aligned DKIM passes DMARC.
issues.fix: Reword `say` to: "A policy tells the receiver whether to monitor, quarantine, or reject mail that does not pass the domain's SPF and DKIM checks, and where to send reports."

issues.problem: 'Attestation confirms users still need what they have' treats attestation only as periodic access review. The Messer video cited as this concept's source describes attestation as verifying a person's identity during identity proofing ('all of this needs to be verified through a process called attestation'). SY0-701 prep sources split on this term, so the note contradicts its own cited source. Same framing is used in rw.sec.iam.next and lesson 25 step 'attest'. The keyed answers still hold because they say 'access reviews', but the definition should acknowledge both senses.
issues.fix: Change line 3 to: "Attestation is formal confirmation: that a person is who they claim to be, and (in access reviews) that their access is still needed." No change needed to the keyed answer of rw.sec.iam.next.

issues.problem: 'Secure cookies protect session data in the browser' is imprecise. The Secure attribute stops the browser sending the cookie over unencrypted HTTP (protection in transit); it does not protect data stored in the browser. This also sits awkwardly beside rw.sec.app.next, which correctly separates Secure (transit) from HttpOnly (script access).
issues.fix: Replace line 2 with: "Secure cookies are sent only over HTTPS, so session tokens are not exposed in transit."

issues.problem: Clue 'When two ports appear together, ask whether the protocol normally uses a client and server pair' is only true for DHCP (67 server / 68 client). FTP 20/21 are data and control channels, and SNMP 161/162 are polling and traps. The port numbers themselves are all correct.
issues.fix: Replace clue with: "Paired ports split a job: FTP 21 control and 20 data, DHCP 67 server and 68 client, SNMP 161 queries and 162 traps."

notes: Read every item in all five files (28 concepts with 56 recall cards, 4 comparisons, 50 scenarios, 6 lessons = 30 sections with 23 practices and 6 casebook cases, 22 exam-style items). Severity totals: {"wrong":1,"ambiguous":1,"minor":17,"giveaway":28}. Structure is clean: every scenario has no.length = o.length-1, every practice and case has exactly one correct option, no match `extra` fits a row, all dd blank counts match, all concept/comparison/lesson cross-references resolve, and each scenario's day/obj matches its concept. Every port number and transport pairing in the batch is correct (20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 and 587 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 161/162 SNMP, 389 LDAP, 443 HTTPS, 445 SMB, 636 LDAPS, 993 IMAPS, 995 POP3S, 3389 RDP). Firewall first-match and implicit-deny logic, incident response order, CVE/CVSS, false positive/negative, SAML/OAuth/OIDC, MFA factor rules, MAC/DAC/RBAC/ABAC, chain of custody and legal hold are all stated correctly, and no keyed answer is wrong. data-cn-sec-3-cmp.js is clean apart from one wording slip. All 29 Professor Messer source URLs exist on the SY0-701 course index. Option order is shuffled at render (index.html), so answer position is not a giveaway; correct-answer length is not systematically biased (13 of 50 scenarios have the longest option correct, about chance). The dominant weakness is distractor quality, not accuracy. Coverage gaps noticed but not listed as issues: no EAP types or WPA2-vs-WPA3 detail, no rule-based access control, no scan types (credentialed vs non-credentialed), no LDAP, no e-discovery/reporting/preservation, no tabletop/simulation or root cause analysis, and no UDP/TCP transport drill in the ports level. Not verified: the official CompTIA objectives PDF could not be fetched directly; objective wording was confirmed from a publisher's SY0-701 guide and Messer's course pages. Whether CVE-2026-1044 is assigned was not looked up.
